title: Analyzing Spanish-Language YouTube Discourse During the 2025 Iberian Peninsula Blackout
screen_reason: Content analysis of 76,398 Spanish-language YouTube comments on the 28 April 2025 Iberian blackout, classified by GPT-4o-mini. Reports the share of comments flagged as containing misinformation (46.1%) against an explicit denominator — a CONTENT prevalence estimate. (The MDPI header labels the item 'Review' but it is an original empirical study with its own data collection.)

estimates.country: Spain / Iberian Peninsula (Spanish-language videos on the 28 April 2025 Spain–Portugal blackout; commenter location not restricted)
estimates.date: Comments on videos published 28 April 2025; comments retrieved 16 May 2025
estimates.measure_type: % of Spanish-language YouTube comments on blackout videos flagged as containing misinformation
estimates.denominator: 76,398 Spanish-language comments from the 360 most relevant YouTube videos published on 28 April 2025 for the search query “apagón”
estimates.definition: Comment classified by GPT-4o-mini as containing or engaging with misleading or false content (categories: false or misleading claims, conspiracy theories, political/ideological misinformation, rumors and speculation, bias and distortion, disinformation and manipulation, scientific misconceptions, inaccuracies, denialism, satire/humor)
estimates.misinfo_def: “Misinformation identification: Detecting comments containing false or misleading information.”
estimates.source_quote: Among all comments, 46.1% are flagged as containing misinformation, indicating that nearly half of the discourse includes or engages with misleading or false content
estimates.ground_truth_detail: OpenAI GPT-4o-mini via the OpenAI API classified every comment; no prompt, codebook, or full-sample validation reported. Partial validation only: 100 randomly selected flagged comments were manually reviewed and 86 were 'clearly identifiable as misinformation', the remainder context-dependent cases and apparent false positives. No inter-rater or agreement statistic.
estimates.moderator_quote: Comments were extracted using the YouTube Data API v3, focusing on videos uploaded on the day of the blackout and most relevant to the search query “apagón” (Spanish for “blackout”). ... A total of 76,398 comments from 360 videos were retrieved on 16 May 2025 ... The OpenAI GPT-4o-mini model, accessed via the OpenAI API, was employed to perform various analyses on the dataset.
estimates.notes: Two coding calls an adjudicator should see. (a) Country: the corpus is Spanish-LANGUAGE videos about a Spain/Portugal event; commenter geography was never restricted or measured, so this could include the wider Spanish-speaking world. Coded Spain because the event, the video corpus and the paper's policy framing (comparison against Spain's CIS survey, recommendations for the Iberian region) are Spain-centred; Global is the defensible alternative. (b) denom_selection=curated because the 360 videos are the 'most relevant' search results, i.e. a rank-truncated set. Topic coded 'other' (infrastructure/disaster crisis event), which fits none of the listed categories cleanly. Ground truth is a general-purpose LLM with only a 100-comment precision spot-check, so the value should be treated as classifier-derived, not human-verified.

SOURCE_QUOTE NOTE: the sentence is split across a page break in the text file (a running header 'Societies 2025, 15, 174 9 of 17' is interpolated mid-sentence, and 'identifiable' is hyphenated across a line), so the quote is the longest exact contiguous span carrying the value. missed_or_uncertain: (1) Misinformation TYPE breakdown (false/misleading claims 40.6%, conspiracy theories 20.0%, political/ideological 17.5%, rumors and speculation 10.5%, bias and distortion 4.0%; Figure 7) — shares within the flagged set of what kind of misinformation it is, not prevalence, so no rows. (2) Misinformation STANCE (70.8% support the false content, 24.6% neutral, 4.6% explicitly oppose; Figure 8) — a within-misinformation stance distribution, not a falsity share. (3) Perceived-cause categories, incl. 'conspiratorial or elite manipulation (8.8%)' and 'external attacks or threats (7.0%)' — these are shares of the 53.8% of comments attributing a cause, i.e. what commenters blamed, not whether the comment was false. (4) All CIS flash-survey figures quoted in the Discussion (52.4% significantly/moderately affected; 21.5% reported fear; ~60% considered government communication insufficient; 26.6% suspected deliberate causes such as cyberattacks) are cited from reference [22], not the paper's own data — excluded under R8. So is the '43% of European citizens used social media for emergency information' figure in the Introduction (ref [3]). (5) Sentiment, emotion, urgency, tone, call-to-action and infrastructure-impact distributions are not misinformation measures.

rob.design: Single-author platform content analysis. Frame: 360 'most relevant' YouTube videos published 28 April 2025 for the query 'apagón' (Spanish only), all 76,398 comments retrieved via YouTube Data API v3 on 16 May 2025. No sampling within the corpus, no response rate (platform data). Classification entirely by OpenAI GPT-4o-mini; no prompt or codebook reported, no inter-rater reliability. Validation limited to manual review of 100 flagged comments (86 confirmed). Author-acknowledged limits: YouTube commenters unrepresentative, Spanish-only, model may miss sarcasm/idiom/context, misinformation detection depends on the model's training data.
